# Jidoka

> Built-in quality for agent instructions. Eight layers each hold one job.
> One command stops the line the moment a layer drifts, a job goes stale, or
> an invariant breaks.

Jidoka is an open-source standard for keeping humans and coding agents on one
layered instruction architecture. The name is the Toyota principle of building
quality into the process itself, so the line stops at the first defect and
never passes one downstream. Instructions span eight layers, ascending from
most general (the system prompt, every run) to most specific (a checklist at
one pause point). Each layer owns a single job, no layer restates another, and
every layer has a machine-checkable budget — so a defect always traces to
exactly one of them, and the checks halt before it ships.

The `jidoka` command family is the andon cord. Three checks each own one
class of defect, so every finding routes to exactly one fix. `jidoka
instructions` gates every layer with a line cap and a word cap, and it fails a
checklist block with too many items or an item that explains. `jidoka jtbd`
validates every job entry against the schema and reports a generated block
that no longer matches its manifest; `--fix` regenerates it. `jidoka
invariants` discovers every `*.rules.mjs` module under `.jidoka/invariants/`
and runs it through one engine. The engine ships with the CLI. The policy
stays in the repository. A rule module names one claim, collects its subjects
with kit helpers such as `grep`, `scan`, `scanAst`, and `restatementDrift`,
and declares rules with an id, a message, and a hint. A finding names the
file, the line, the rule id, and the fix. Every command accepts `--json` for
machine-readable findings.

The standard draws on Jidoka (Toyota) for how quality holds, Jobs To Be Done
(Christensen, Moesta) for what agents align to, and The Checklist Manifesto
(Gawande) for how alignment holds under load.

The lowest layer, verification, uses two checklist gates. Each is wrapped in
a semantic tag — `<read_do_checklist>` for entry gates, `<do_confirm_checklist>`
for exit gates — so every pause point in a repository is discoverable from
anywhere with one `rg` search.

Jidoka stands on its own: any well-structured repository can adopt it,
whatever its directory shape. It defines the universal root files every
adopting repository carries — CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and JTBD.md — along
with the Jobs To Be Done conventions. A repository's structure standard extends
it; the Monorepo standard is one such extension, and the Kata Agent Team
implements it as a daily loop.

Install the skill pack via `apm install forwardimpact/jidoka-skills` and the
CLI via `npm install --save-dev @forwardimpact/jidoka`, then ask Claude to set
it up. Wire `npx jidoka` and `npx jidoka invariants` into your checks to stop
the line at the first drifted layer. The bare command runs the layer and jobs
checks. Only the second call runs the repository's own rule modules.

The documentation tree covers adoption, the layer architecture, and the checks.
Getting Started takes a repository of unlayered prompt files to a check that
stops the line on a deliberate breach. Put Your Instructions on One Layered
Architecture covers what each layer owns, when it loads, and what budget holds
it, then splits into authoring one layer, writing a checklist gate, and writing
a jobs entry. Stop the Line on Instruction Drift covers the check wiring in a
local script and in CI, how to read a finding, how to route each finding to the
fix that owns it, and how to enforce a repository's own invariant rules. The
layers sit inside a repository structure standard at https://www.monorepo.team/,
and the Kata Agent Team at https://www.kata.team/ runs on them every day.
